Pigeonhole Equal Subset Sum: Subexponential Algorithm, Tight Lower Bounds, and Average-Case Analysis **Abstract** The Equal Subset Sum problem asks, given _n_ positive integers bounded by _M_, to find two distinct non-empty subsets with the same sum. We study this problem in the regime _M_=2_o(n_), where the pigeonhole principle guarantees that a solution exists, and the main challenge is to find one efficiently. A straightforward dynamic-programming algorithm runs in time \(\mathrm{poly}(n)\cdot M\), and after a sequence of improvements, the current best algorithm, due to Jin, Williams, and Zhang (ESA 2025), achieves running time \(\mathrm{poly}(n)\cdot M^{1/3}\). In this work, we give the first \(\mathrm{poly}(n)\cdot M^{o(1)}\)-time algorithm for Equal Subset Sum in the regime _M_=2_o(n_). We complement this algorithmic result with a tight conditional lower bound showing that any substantial improvement would require a major breakthrough in approximation algorithms for lattice problems, building on recent techniques of Vafa and Vaikuntanathan (S 2025). Finally, we show that our techniques yield an asymptotically faster algorithm for the regime when \(M=\Theta(2^n)\): a \(\mathrm{poly}(n)\cdot 2^{n/4}\)-time algorithm in the average case. ## 1 Introduction Equal Subset Sum is a fundamental problem in combinatorial optimization. The problem can be stated as follows: given a set _S_ of _n_ positive integers bounded by _M_, find two distinct subsets \(A,B\subseteq S\) such that \(\Sigma(A)=\Sigma(B)\), where \(\Sigma(\cdot)\) denotes the sum of the integers in the set. <tbc>standard meet-in-the-middle algorithm solves the problem in O_<sup>⋆</sup>_(3<sup>_n/_2</sup>), which can be improved to O_<sup>⋆</sup>_(1.7067_<sup>n</sup>_) \[MNPW19\].<sup>1</sup>

Papadimitriou \[Pap94\] introduced the total variant called the _Pigeonhole Equal Subset Sum_ (PESS). In this variant, the sum of the numbers is less than 2_<sup>n</sup>_-1, and the goal remains to find distinct subsets \(A,B\subseteq S\) with equal sums. Since there are 2_<sup>n</sup>_-1 non-empty subsets but only 2_<sup>n</sup>_-2 possible nonzero sums, a collision must exist by the pigeonhole principle. PESS belongs to the class TFNP and, more specifically, to PPP, and it is conjectured to be PPP-complete \[Pap94\]. The setting, when the number of collisions is even larger, e.g., the sum of integers is bounded by 2<sup>_n_-1</sup>, is called _weak-pigeonhole regime_ and is also an important setting \[SZZ18\]. In that weaker setting, PESS belongs to the class PWPP (problems whose totality is proven through the weak pigeonhole principle) \[SZZ18\]. For convenience, we will consider the variants where each of the numbers is bounded by either (2_<sup>n</sup>_-1)_/n_ or 2<sup>_n_-1</sup>_/n_, so the sum remains bounded by 2_<sup>n</sup>_-1 or 2<sup>_n_-1</sup>. To this effect, we introduce a parameter _M_ that denotes the bound on the integers we allow in our instances.

To the best of our knowledge, the first explicit algorithm for PESS was given by Vasilakis \[Vas22\], who obtained an \(\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(nM)\) time dynamic programming algorithm<sup>2</sup>. Allcock, Hamoudi, Joux, Klingelhöfer and Santha \[AHJ<sup>+</sup>22\] gave an O_<sup>⋆</sup>_(2<sup>_n/_2</sup>)-time algorithm when the sum of the numbers is less than 2_<sup>n</sup>_-1. Notice that by discarding the largest items until we reach a modified instance with \(n'\) items whose sum is in \([2^{n^\prime-1}-1,2^{n^\prime}-1)\) and then running the algorithm of Allcock et al. \[AHJ<sup>+</sup>22\], the overall running-time can be presented as O_<sup>⋆</sup>(M_<sup>1/2</sup>). Later, Jin and Wu \[JW24\] refined the meet-in-the-middle approach of \[AHJ<sup>+</sup>22\] and achieved O_<sup>⋆</sup>(M_<sup>0.4</sup>) running time. The current best algorithm by Jin, Williams, and Zhang (ESA 2025) runs in O_<sup>⋆</sup>(M_<sup>1/3</sup>) \[JWZ25\] (see  1 for an overview). At the end of their paper, Jin, Williams, and Zhang raised the question of whether the _M_<sup>1/3</sup> barrier can be improved \[JWZ25\].

**Open Question 1** (\[JWZ25\])**.** _Can we get a_ \(\mathrm{poly}(n)\cdot M^{1/3-\varepsilon}\)_-time algorithm for Pigeonhole Equal Subset Sum for some_ \(\varepsilon>0\)?

Note that PESS is a total problem and, as such, is not expected to be NP-hard. As noted above, it lies in PPP. Inspired by these questions, Jin \[Jin24\] asked whether subexponential-time algorithms for PESS are possible:

**Open Question 2** (\[Jin24, JW24\])**.** _Can we get a subexponential-time algorithm for Pigeonhole Equal Subset Sum?_

More specifically, Jin \[Jin24\] asked for 2<sup>_o(n_)</sup>-time algorithm, which in parameterization by maximum integer can be expressed as \(\mathrm{poly}(n)\cdot M^{o(1)}\).

## 1.1 Our Results

In this work, we make partial progress on both of these questions. First, we present a \(\mathrm{poly}(n)\cdot M^{o(1)}\) - time algorithm for PESS in the regime _M_=2<sup>_o(n_)</sup>.

**Theorem 1.1.** _There exists a deterministic algorithm that, given an integer n and a set_ \(S\subseteq\{1,\dots,M\}\) _of size n such that nM\<_2_<sup>n</sup>_-1_, runs in time_ \(\mathrm{poly}(n)\cdot M^{\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(1/\mathrm{log}\delta)}\) _and returns two distinct subsets of S with the same sum, where_ \(\delta=\delta(n,M):=n/\mathrm{log}M\) _is the density of the instance._

_As a corollary, when M_=2<sup>_o(n_)</sup>_, the algorithm runs in time_ \(\mathrm{poly}(n)\cdot M^{o(1)}\).

<sup>1</sup>\(\mathcal{O}^\star(\cdot)\) and \(\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\cdot)\) hide polynomial and polylogarithmic factors in the input respectively. <sup>2</sup>More precisely, algorithm of Vasilakis \[Vas22\] runs in \(\mathcal{O}(n+\Sigma(S)\mathrm{log}(\Sigma(S)))\) time, where \(\Sigma(S)\) is the sum of the input integers.

Although the algorithm in Theorem 1.1 does not fully resolve Problem 2, we believe it provides significant progress on that question. Notice, that Theorem 1.1 also does not resolve Problem 1, however, more precise running time analysis of Theorem 1.1 shows that it improves the O_<sup>⋆</sup>(M_<sup>1/3</sup>) time algorithm [JWZ25] when \(\delta>19\) (see Remark 1 for an exact runtime). Later in Theorem 1.3 we show that techniques behind Theorem 1.1 can be used to improve state-of-the-art for \(\delta\ge 1\) in the average-case regime.

One could ask whether the \(\mathcal{O}(1/\mathrm{log}\delta)\) term in the exponent can be significantly improved; for example, can we get 2<sup>O(_n_<sup>0.99</sup>)</sup> time, or at least 2<sup>O(_n/_log<sup>100</sup>_n_)</sup> time? We show that this is highly unlikely.

**Theorem 1.2.** _Under Hypothesis 1, there is no_ 2<sup>_o(n/_log_n_)</sup> _time algorithm that solves Pigeonhole Equal Subset Sum. Moreover, there is no_ \(\mathrm{poly}(n)\cdot M^{o(1/\mathrm{log}n)}\) _time algorithm for PESS_ (_even for_ \(\delta=n^{1/2+o(1)}\)).

This lower bound implies that the running time in Theorem 1.1 cannot be improved to \(M^{o(1/\mathrm{log}\delta)}\), and that our algorithm is optimal for polynomial \(\delta\) up to constants in the exponent. We also show a lower bound that excludes a 2<sup>_o(n/_log_n_)</sup> time algorithm for PESS, which conditionally completes our answer to Problem 2 (up to a single log_n_ factor in the exponent). See Figure 2 for an overview of our results.

Theorem 1.2 is conditioned on the hardness of lattice problems. Shortest Vector Problem is a fundamental hardness assumption. For a tunable parameter \(\kappa\ge 1\) and dimension _n_, one can obtain an \(n^\kappa\)-approximation in \(2^{\mathcal{O}(n/\kappa)}\) time [Sch87] and after a substantial effort over the past 40 years (see, e.g., [Sch87, SE94, GN08, ALNSD20]), no 2<sup>_o(n_)</sup> algorithm is known that would yield polynomial approximation for SVP. Significant improvements over these trade-offs would break modern cryptosystems and have been already assumed by Vafa–Vaikuntanathan [VV25] to establish hardness of _symmetric binary perceptron, number partitioning problem_ and more. Here, we consider a stronger, fine-grained version of their assumption <sup>3</sup>:

**Hypothesis 1.** _For any constant_ \(c\ge 1\)_, there exists_ \(\varepsilon>0\) _such that there is no_ \(\mathcal{O}(2^{\varepsilon n})\) _time algorithm that given an n-dimensional lattice_ L _with high probability returns a non-zero vector_ \(\mathbf{v}\in\mathcal{L}\) _such that_ \(\|\mathbf{v}\|_2\le\mathcal{O}(n^c)\cdot\lambda_n(\mathcal{L})\).

We show that lack of 2<sup>_o(n_)</sup>-time polynomial approximation for this problem is a major obstacle to improve our \(M^{\mathcal{O}(1/\mathrm{log}\delta)}\)-time algorithm for PESS. We stress that Hypothesis 1 is not a standard complexity assumption, and to the best of our knowledge, we are the first ones to use it in that form. Regardless of whether one believes in Hypothesis 1 or not, our message is as follows:

_To improve the running time of Theorem 1.1, one would need first to make a substantial breakthrough for lattice problems._

Finally, we focus on the case \(M\le 2^n\). <sup>4</sup> The average-case setting is an important relaxation in which the algorithm is required to work correctly on most inputs rather than on every input. This perspective is relevant for both practical and theoretical reasons. For example, average-case algorithms for Subset Sum have been widely studied and play an important role in cryptography, since such instances were long considered as hardness assumptions [MH78, Sha84]. Understanding the average-case complexity of Subset Sum, therefore, matters for both practice and theory [LO85b, HGJ10, BCJ11, LO85a, CJL<sup>+</sup>92, DDKS12]. Motivated by this, we present an O_<sup>⋆</sup>(M_<sup>1/4</sup>)-time algorithm for equal Subset Sum in the average-case setting when \(M\le 2^n\).

<sup>3</sup>Formally, Hypothesis 1 concerns an important variant of the problem called _n_-th Successive Minima Problem. <sup>4</sup>The algorithm in the average case works even for density less than 1, when \(M=\Theta(n^\kappa\cdot 2^n)\) for some \(\kappa>0\); the only caveat is that the success probability decreases with increasing \(\kappa\).

**Theorem 1.3.** _Let_ \(M=\Theta\left(2^n\right)\)_. There exists a deterministic algorithm that given a set A of n random integers sampled uniformly from the set_ {1_,...,M}, finds distinct_ \(X,Y\subseteq A\) _such that_ \(\Sigma(X)=\Sigma(Y)\) _with probability_ \(\Omega\left(n^{-2}\right)\) _in_ \(\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(2^{n/4})\) _time._

Note that this result holds in the _average case_, whereas previous work guaranteed solutions in the worst case. The algorithm is a modification of the algorithm behind Theorem 1.1; however, the analysis is much more involved. Curiously, we can show that our algorithm also works for the _modular version_ of Equal Subset Sum. In that setting, the best algorithm is due to Allcock et al. \[AHJ<sup>+</sup>22\], who gave an O_<sup>⋆</sup>(M_<sup>1/2</sup>)-time algorithm. In fact, obtaining a faster algorithm in the modular setting is posed as an open question in \[Jin24\].

**Theorem 1.4.** _Let the modulus_ \(M=\Theta\left(2^n\right)\)_, where M=pqr,_ \(p,q=\Theta\left(M^{1/4}\right)\) _and p, q, and r are pairwise co-prime integers. There exists a deterministic algorithm that given a set A of n random modular integers sampled uniformly from_ Z_<sub>M</sub>, finds distinct_ \(X,Y\subseteq A\) _such that_ \(\Sigma(X)\equiv_M\Sigma(Y)\) _with probability_ \(\Omega\left(1\right)\) _in_ \(\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(2^{n/4})\) _time._

Notice that in this setting, we require _M_ to be a product of three pairwise co-prime integers, but the probability of success is higher. If the modulus is not a product of such integers, then using Theorem 1.3, trivially we can solve the modular problem with success probability \(\Omega(n^{-2})\). A faster average-case algorithm often leads to improved worst-case algorithms. This happened for Subset Balancing, a generalization of Equal Subset Sum, where recent average-case results \[CJRS22\] motivated improved worst-case algorithms \[RW26\]. Because our analysis is already quite technical in the average-case setting, we hope it will eventually yield worst-case algorithms with comparable running time. Note that the algorithm behind Theorem 1.1 is deterministic, albeit less efficient for small densities. In the following figure, we summarize all our results with the related previous work.

## 2 Our Techniques

### 2.1 Technique behind Theorem 1.1

#### Ingredient 1: Dynamic Programming.

**Ingredient 2: Differencing Algorithm.** Next, we reformulate the classical differencing technique of Karmarkar-Karp \[KK82\]. Although originally designed for partitioning in the average-case setting, the differencing strategy can be adapted to the Equal Subset Sum setting even in the worst-case setting. It gives a polynomial-time algorithm when integers are bounded by _M_=2<sup>_c_log<sup>2</sup>_n_</sup> for a small constant _c\>_0. We reinterpret this procedure as follows:

Let 0_\<a_<sub>1</sub>_\<...\<a<sub>n</sub>_ be the sorted input numbers and, for simplicity, assume that _n_ is a power of 2. For every \(i\in[n/2]\), define \(\Delta_i:=a_{2i}-a_{2i-1}\), the difference between the two consecutive numbers in the _i_-th pair (note that \(\Delta_i\ge 0\)). We call \(i\in[n/2]\) _good_ if \(\Delta_i\le 4M/n\), and _bad_ otherwise.

Observe that there are at least _n/_4 good pairs. Indeed, if there were more than _n/_4 bad indices, then \(\sum_{i\in\mathrm{bad}}\Delta_i>|\mathrm{bad}|\cdot\frac{4M}{n}>M\), which contradicts the fact that \(\sum_{i\in[n/2]}\Delta_i<a_n\le M\).

Now observe the following: if we discard bad indices, we obtain at least _n/_4 numbers whose values decreased by a factor _n/_4. If we repeat this for \(\kappa=\Theta(\mathrm{log}n)\) rounds, we get a number whose value is bounded by \(\le M\cdot(\frac{4}{n})^\kappa<1\) for sufficiently small constant \(c\in(0,1/4]\). <sup>5</sup> Therefore, eventually, we must observe integer zero, because throughout the procedure, the numbers are nonnegative integers.

The key combinatorial observation is that the sign chosen in the last \(\Delta_i\) determines to which subset the corresponding element _a<sub>i</sub>_ belongs in the final solution. Hence, an integer zero naturally corresponds to two different subsets of the same sum.

**Combining the ingredients.** Karmarkar-Karp differencing approach already has several applications in cryptology. Importantly for us, Wagner \[Wag02\] extended it to solve _the k-list problem_ in the average-case setting (see also an independent work of \[BKW03\]). Similarly to these works, we also combine dynamic programming with the Karmarkar-Karp differencing approach. Somehow surprisingly, in comparison to these approaches, our algorithm is deterministic and works in the worst case.

Let _k_ be a largest integer such that \(M\le k^{n/(4k)}\). For simplicity, let us assume that _k_ is a power of 2 and _k_ divides _n_ and let _W_:=2<sup>_n/_(2_k_)</sup> (in Section 4 we give tighter bounds). We start by partitioning the input into _k_ equal blocks and precompute the list of all subset sums inside each block to obtain sets \(\mathcal{A}_i^{(0)}\) for each \(i\in[k]\). Rather than matching high-order bits (as in the differencing approach), we repeatedly merge blocks and keep large sumsets that share the same low-order bits, i.e., we work modulo _W<sup>j</sup>_ in level _j_.

More precisely, at each level _j_=1,2_,...,_log_k_ we maintain sets \(\mathcal{A}_i^{(j)}\) for every \(i\in[k/2^j]\). The sets \(\mathcal{A}_i^{(j)}\) arise by _merging_ two sets \(\mathcal{A}_{2i-1}^{(j-1)}\) and \(\mathcal{A}_{2i}^{(j-1)}\) from the previous levels. Merging is performed by taking the sumset \(\mathcal{A}_{2i-1}^{(j-1)}+\mathcal{A}_{2i}^{(j-1)}\).<sup>6</sup> Notice that the size of that set increases; therefore, we need to _prune_ it. We achieve it by partitioning the sumset into _W_ sets of integers based on their value modulo _W<sup>j</sup>_ and keeping a representative subset of size exactly _W_ from the largest set. This pruning keeps the lists to have size exactly _W_ while maintaining a large ensemble of sums whose lowest bits agree (see Algorithm 1).

We include the full proof of Theorem 1.1 in Section 4. ## 2.2 Techniques behind Theorem 1.2 Very recently, the connection between the Karmarkar-Karp differencing method and lattice problems was highlighted by Vafa and Vaikuntanathan \[VV25\]. Their work studies an average-case version of the _Number Partitioning Problem_ (NPP), where one is given a random vector **a**=(_a_1_,...,an_)∼N(**0**,**I**_n_) and the goal is to find a vector \(\mathbf{x}\in\{-1,1\}^n\) such that \(\left|\mathbf{a}^\top\mathbf{x}\right|\le\kappa(n)\sqrt{n}\). They prove a worst-case-to-average-case reduction from the lattice problem _Incremental Guaranteed Distance Decoding_ (IncGDD) to NPP. In particular, they show that an average-case polynomial- time algorithm for NPP achieving \(\kappa(n)=2^{-\Omega(\mathrm{log}^{3+\varepsilon} n)}\) would contradict their assumed subexponential hardness of approximate lattice problems \[VV25\] including the Shortest Independent Vector Problem (SIVP) (see Hypothesis 2). Thus, under these assumptions, Karmarkar-Karp is nearly optimal in polynomial time. They also note that their reduction extends to related variants, including the _Number Balancing Problem_ (NBP) where the Gaussian distribution is replaced with the uniform distribution on \[0,1\] and solution vectors are {-1,0,1}_n_\\{**0**} \[VV25\]. At a high level, one may view NBP as closely related to an equal-sum type problem after an appropriate discretization of the input numbers. In particular, if the target error is \(\kappa(n)\), then the relevant integer range after scaling is roughly of magnitude \(1/\kappa(n)\). This suggests that the hardness result of \[VV25\] is consistent with the absence of polynomial-time algorithms for average-case PESS when \(M\approx\frac{1}{\kappa(n)}=2^{\Omega(\mathrm{log}^{3+\varepsilon} n)}\). Consequently, this also provides evidence against polynomial-time algorithms for the corre **Algorithm 1:** Algorithm behind Theorem 1.1.

## Technique behind our lower bound.

Inspired by the above, we show a connection between lattice problems and PESS. We achieve a tight lower bound, but in comparison to \[VV25\]: (i) we work only in the worst-case setting, (ii) we only show lower bounds against subexponential time algorithms, and (iii) Hypothesis 1 is much stronger than the assumptions in \[VV25\] (see discussion in Section 3).

Our reduction is from _n<sup>th</sup>-Successive Minima Problem_ (nSMP) (see Definition 4). The task in nSMP<sup>7</sup> is to find a nonzero lattice vector \(\mathbf{v}\in\mathcal{L}\) such that \(\|\mathbf{v}\|_2\le\lambda_n(\mathcal{L})\). By Theorem B.3, this formulation is equivalent (up to an irrelevant to us loss in approximation), to the approximate SIVP.

At a high level, the reduction is motivated by the classical sieve of Ajtai, Kumar, and Sivakumar \[AKS01\] for obtaining a short vector. However, our proof does not literally simulate a sieve. Instead, it samples many lattice vectors, encodes them as positive integers, invokes the assumed black-box PESS algorithm on the resulting instance, and decodes the returned equal-sum collision into a short lattice vector. Thus, PESS plays the role of a collision-finding primitive analogous in spirit to the sieve step.

More concretely, on input we are given an _n_-dimensional lattice L and we will use hypothetical _M_<sup>_o_(1/log_N_)</sup>-time algorithm that solves PESS on instances with \(N=\Theta(n^2)\) integers bounded by _M_=2<sup>O(_n_log_n_)</sup>. We start by preprocessing an _n_-dimensional lattice L. First, we compute a short basis **D**. If we use the state-of-the-art algorithms (e.g., \[Sch87, ALNSD20\]) in time \(\mathcal{O}(2^{\varepsilon n})\) we can compute a basis of length \(B\cdot\lambda_n(\mathcal{L})\), where \(B=n^{\Theta(1/\varepsilon)}\) for any tunable \(\varepsilon>0\). Next, we sample independent lattice points **x**<sup>(1)</sup>_,...,_**x**<sup>(_N_)</sup>∼_D_<sub>L_,s_</sub> using the (good) basis **D** generated in the first step, for a suitable Gaussian parameter \(s=\Theta(\sqrt{n}N\|\mathbf{D}\|_2)\). Standard tail bounds imply that, except with negligible probability, all sampled vectors satisfy<tbc>

\(\left\|\mathbf{x}^{(i)}\right\|_\infty\le BN^2\lambda_n(\mathcal{L})\text{for every}i\in[N].\)

<tbc>We then encode each sampled vector as a positive integer using a base-_W_ representation, where \(W=\Theta(BN^3)\). Schematically, the encoding has the form

\(a_i=W^n+\sum_{j=1}^nW^{j-1}\left\lfloor\frac{(\mathbf{x}^{(i)})_j/\lambda_n(\mathcal{L})}{r_j}\right\rfloor,\)

where each _r<sub>j</sub>_ is a random prime in \[_N_<sup>3</sup>\]; in the actual proof, we also add independent random shifts before rounding to ensure all integers are different with high probability. The additive term _W<sup>n</sup>_ ensures positivity, while the choice of _W_ is large enough to prevent carries between coordinates. Strictly speaking, the reduction does not know \(\lambda_n(\mathcal{L})\) in advance. Instead, it guesses this quantity up to a factor of 2 by enumerating powers of two, and for the correct guess obtains \(\widetilde{\lambda}_n\) satisfying \(\lambda_n(\mathcal{L})\le\widetilde{\lambda}_n\le 2\lambda_n(\mathcal{L})\) (similarly to Ajtai et al. \[AKS01\]). Accordingly, the encoding uses \(\widetilde{\lambda}_n\) in place of \(\lambda_n(\mathcal{L})\).

Since each coordinate contributes only O(_BN_<sup>2</sup>) to a digit, every encoded integer is at most _M_=(_BN_)<sup>O(_n_)</sup>. We partition the _n_ input integers into four equal blocks, enumerate all subset sums inside each block, and then perform two rounds of merging: first modulo _p_, and then modulo _q_. Thus, in both settings, the output of the filtering stage is a final list of subset sums that agree modulo _pq_. This agreement modulo _pq_ is only an intermediate condition. In the modular setting, to obtain a collision modulo _M=pqr_, one must additionally ensure collision in the residual _r_-part, after which the Chinese Remainder Theorem yields a collision modulo _M_. In the integer setting, agreement modulo _pq_ again controls only the low-order bits, and one must additionally understand carry propagation and the remaining high-order contribution. Thus, the main difference lies not in the algorithmic template, but in its analysis - in particular, the analysis of the collision variable that denotes the number of collisions in the final list. The modular setting is relatively simpler, due to uniform distributions, CRT, and modular arithmetic. Whereas in the integer setting, even the first-moment calculation of the collision variable becomes substantially more intricate. Nevertheless, the modular analysis remains crucial. As we will see later, controlling the success probability requires a second-moment bound, and in the integer case, this is obtained by comparison with the more tractable modular collision variable.

For simplicity, here, we assume that the input integer bound/modulus _M=pqr_, where \(2^{n-1}\le M\le 2^n\), \(p,q\in[2^{n/4-1},2^{n/4}]\), and _p_, _q_, and _r_ are pairwise co-prime integers. The reason lies in the complexity of the different levels of our algorithm (see below), which is proportional to the sizes of the integers _p_ and _q_ used in the filtering steps. To balance this complexity, the modulus must contain two distinct prime factors of size approximately _M_<sup>1/4</sup>. The remaining factor, denoted by _r_, accounts for the rest of the modulus. Moreover, requiring the factors to be pairwise coprime is essential to apply the Chinese Remainder Theorem.

To analyze this common filtering procedure, we introduce collision-counting random variables and study their first and second moments. ## Distribution of collisions. Now, we aim to analyze the distribution of integer and modular collisions in the final list _L_1234. For this, we first define two random variables that denote the number of non-trivial integer and modular collisions in this final list. Let C(int) and C(pqr) denote these two random variables, respectively. Our filtering algorithm succeeds if the value of these variables is at least 1. Hence, we look for the probability of this event. For any input instance, we can compute the value of C(int), and similarly C(pqr), by iterating through all the possible pairs of binary vectors, and considering whether the vectors (or the corresponding subset sum) pass through the filters of the algorithm and collide, over integers or modulo _pqr_, based on the problem. For each pair of binary vectors **u**_i,_**u**_j_, we define a binary random variable \(\mathcal{C}_{ij}^{(\mathrm{int})}\) and \(\mathcal{C}_{ij}^{(\mathrm{pqr})}\), such that their value is 1 if and only if **u**_i_ and **u**_j_ pass through all the filters of the algorithm, and they collide over integers or modulo _r_ based on the problem. ## First Moment. In the modular case, we have that the probability of vectors **u**_i_ and **u**_j_ surviving the algorithm is 1_/p_4_q_2 8, and the probability of them colliding modulo _r_ is 1_/r_, given \(\mathbf{u}_i\neq\mathbf{u}_j\). Hence, we have \(\mathbb{E}_\mathbf{a}\left(\mathcal{C}_{ij}^{(\mathrm{pqr})}\right)=1/p^4q^2r\). Since there are \(\Theta(4^n)\) pairs of binary vectors, using the bounds for _M,p_, and _q_, we have \(\mathbb{E}_\mathbf{a}\left(\mathcal{C}^{(\mathrm{pqr})}\right)=\Omega(1)\) (see Section 6 for details). Next, we focus on the integer case. The vectors surviving the algorithm and their collision over the remaining bits are dependent on each other. Hence, the analysis of the first moment in this case is a bit involved. We split the integer subset sum as follows: \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{u}_i=\left(\mathbf{a}^{(pq)}+\mathbf{a}^{(r)}\cdot pq\right)\cdot\mathbf{u}_i,\)
\(=\underbrace{\mathbf{a}^{(pq)}\cdot\mathbf{u}_i\mathrm{mod}pq}_{pq\text{bits}}+\underbrace{\mathbf{a}^{(pq)}\cdot\mathbf{u}_i-\left(\mathbf{a}^{(pq)}\cdot\mathbf{u}_i\mathrm{mod}pq\right)}_{pq\text{carry bits}}\cdot pq+\underbrace{\mathbf{a}^{(r)}\cdot\mathbf{u}_i}_{\text{remaining bits}}\cdot pq.\) To make the analysis simpler, also since we are only interested in the lower bound of the first moment, we redefine the random variable \(\mathcal{C}_{ij}^{(\mathrm{int})}\) as follows: its value is 1 if and only if **u**_i,_**u**_j_ survive filtering algorithm, they collide over the carry bits, and the remaining bits separately. Since the vectors **a**(_pq_) and **a**(_r_) are independent, we can analyze the corresponding sums separately. To characterize the distribution of the sum of integer-valued random variables, we employ the Local Central Limit Theorem (LCLT) \[IL65, MU17\]. Informally, the LCLT asserts that the distribution of the sum of I.I.D. random variables converges to a discrete Gaussian distribution, and that in a neighborhood of the mean, the point probabilities are approximately uniform up to constant factors. To apply this result in our setting, we restrict attention to binary vectors whose Hamming weight is \(\Theta(n)\). A formal statement of the theorem is provided in Section 7. Leveraging the smoothness of the sum distributions, we first show that the carry bits converge in distribution to a discrete normal distribution, and henceforth we prove that the total sum modulo _pq_ and the left sum modulo _p_ condition on the carry bits converges to the uniform distribution asymptotically. Finally, we show that the following three events _E_1_,E_2 and _E_3 are asymptotically independent, where \(E_1:=\sum_{j=1}^{n/2}a_j^{(pq)}\cdot u_{ij}\equiv_p\alpha,E_2:=\mathbf{a}^{(pq)}\cdot\mathbf{u}_i\equiv_{pq}\beta\), and \(E_3:=\left\lfloor\mathbf{a}^{(pq)}\cdot\mathbf{u}_i/pq\right\rfloor=\gamma\). Combining this result and using the Local Central Limit Theorem again for the remaining bits, we have \(\mathbb{E}_\mathbf{a}\left(\mathcal{C}_{ij}^{(\mathrm{int})}\right)=\Omega(1/(np^4q^2r))\). At this point, we know that the expected number of collisions is positive (and in the modular case, even bounded away from 0). However, a lower bound on E\[C\] alone does not imply that the algorithm succeeds on a typical input. Indeed, a random variable can have expectation 1 while being 0 with overwhelming probability and very large on a tiny exceptional set. Thus, the first moment identifies only the correct _scale_ of the number of collisions; by itself, it _does not_ yield a lower bound on P\[C_\>_0\]. Therefore, to prove that the filtering algorithm succeeds with substantial probability, it is essential to control the second moment of C. This is precisely why our analysis focuses on bounding E\[C2\], and, in the integer case, why we first pass through the more tractable modular variable C(_pqr_) in Section 6. As discussed above, analyzing \(\mathcal{C}_{ij}^{(\mathrm{int})}\) directly is challenging because of the interaction between pseudo-uniform distributions and carry propagation. In particular, obtaining a useful upper bound on its second moment appears substantially _more delicate_ than in the modular setting. However, since \(\mathcal{C}_{ij}^{(\mathrm{int})}\le\mathcal{C}_{ij}^{(\mathrm{pqr})}\) and our goal is to upper-bound the second moment, it is enough to study the second moment of \(\mathcal{C}_{ij}^{(\mathrm{pqr})}\) instead!9 This modular quantity is considerably more tractable, since it can be analyzed using the structural advantages of the Chinese Remainder Theorem and modular arithmetic. Thus, the modular case is not merely a warm-up: it provides the key input for controlling the second moment, and hence the success probability, in the integer setting. Next, we explain how to compute the second moment C(pqr). The second moment of C(pqr) can be written as follows (we replace C(pqr) with C for the ease of presentation): \(\mathbb{E}_\mathbf{a}\left(\mathcal{C}^2\right)=\mathbb{E}_\mathbf{a}\left(\sum\mathcal{C}_{ij}\cdot\sum\mathcal{C}_{\ell k}\right)\)
\(=\sum_{i \(=\sum_{(i,j)\neq(\ell,k)}\mathbb{P}_\mathbf{a}\left(\mathcal{C}_{ij}=1\wedge\mathcal{C}_{\ell k}=1\right)+\mathbb{E}_\mathbf{a}\left(\mathcal{C}\right)\) The main difficulty in analyzing the second moment stems from dependencies between events induced by linear relationships among the binary vectors. To address this issue, we partition the set _S_ of all possible 4-tuples of binary vectors into cells such that, for every tuple within a given cell, the joint probability \(\mathbb{P}_\mathbf{a}(\mathcal{C}_{ij}=1\wedge\mathcal{C}_{\ell k}=1)\), admits a uniform upper bound, while the size of each cell can also be tightly bounded. This structured partitioning allows us to control the contribution of dependent events to the second moment. The construction and analysis of these cells rely on a combination of linear-algebraic and combinatorial techniques. ### Complexity Analysis.

The complexity analysis of the algorithm boils down to computing the expected sizes of the list generated by the algorithm. A crucial observation is that the algorithm only depends on the random variable **a**<sup>(_pq_)</sup>. Now, if **a**<sup>(_pq_)</sup> is uniformly distributed over \(\mathbb{Z}_{pq}^n\) then \(\mathbf{a}^{(pq)}\cdot\mathbf{u}\) modulo _pq_ is uniformly distributed over Z_<sub>pq</sub>_, given \(\mathbf{u}\in\{0,1\}^n\backslash\{0^n\}\). Using similar arguments, we can say that in both the modular and the integer case, subset sums mod _p_ and _q_ are uniformly distributed over Z_<sub>p</sub>_ and Z_<sub>q</sub>_ respectively. Therefore, the probability of any subset surviving the first level is 1_/p_<sup>2</sup>=1/2<sup>_n/_2</sup> (1_/p_ for each constraint), and it reaching the second level is 1_/p_<sup>2</sup>_q_=1/2<sup>3_n/_4</sup>. And, since there are 2_<sup>n</sup>_ subsets in total, the expected size of the final list is 2<sup>_n/_4</sup>. Using similar arguments, we conclude that the expected sizes of the lists _L_<sub>12</sub> and _L_<sub>34</sub> are also 2<sup>_n/_4</sup>.

To the best of our knowledge, this is the first fine-grained average-case analysis for Equal Subset Sum (with density 1) that combines two-round Wagner-style pruning with an explicit second- moment argument. We further conjecture that the same viewpoint may eventually extend to the worst-case setting, once combined with the structural ideas developed by Jin and Wu [JW24]. We also conjecture that by using the randomness available in the filtering algorithm, i.e., choosing the bins modulo _p_ and _q_ uniformly randomly rather fixed values, we can improve the success probability to 1-_o_(1).

### 2.4 Related Work

Ajtai [Ajt96] showed that an \(\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{n})\)-approximation to Minkowski’s vector problem would yield an O(_n_)-approximation to the Shortest Vector problem. Hoberg et al. [HRRY17] showed connection between Number Balancing Problem and Minkowski. In the setting of Pigeonhole Equal Subset Sum, their result implies that a polynomial-time algorithm when the sum of the integers is \(2^{n-\sqrt{n}}\) would yield a polynomial approximation to the Shortest Vector Problem in polynomial time.

There has been a significant interest in analyzing the Subset Sum in restricted regimes or under average-case assumptions. The classical result by Lagarias and Odlyzko [LO85b] shows that Subset Sum can be solved in polynomial time on average when the input lies in the low-density regime. This line of work has had cryptographic implications, particularly in attacking knapsack- based cryptosystems, and has led to further developments [CJL<sup>+</sup>92, HGJ10, BCJ11, JW26]. More recently, Agrawalet al. [ASS<sup>+</sup>24] presented a new algorithm for average-case _k_-XOR problems at low densities.

With regard to reductions from variants of the Subset Sum problem to lattice problems, van Emde Boas [vEB81] gave a reduction from Equal Sum to the Closest Vector Problem (CVP). A standard reduction from ordinary Subset Sum to CVP is explicitly presented by Micciancio [Mic02]. Krishnamoorthy, Webb, and Moyer [KWM12] reduced a decisional version of a variant of the Number Partitioning Problem to CVP. Yu and Xiao [YX18] reduced multi-dimensional modular subset sum to the Bounded Distance Decoding problem. Dutta and Rajasree [DR23] showed that Unbounded Subset Sum reduces to CVP under the \(\ell_1\) and \(\ell_\infty\) norms. More recently, Hittmeir [Hit25] gave a reduction from a constrained variant of Subset Sum to the gap variant of Shortest Vector Problem.

## 3.1 Lattices

A lattice L is the set of all integer combinations of linearly independent vectors \(\mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_2,\dots,\mathbf{b}_n\in\mathbb{R}^d\):

\(\mathcal{L}=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^nz_i\mathbf{b}_i|z_i\in\mathbb{Z}\right\}\)

where _n_ is called the rank of the lattice, and _d_ is the dimension. The vectors **b**<sub>1</sub>,**b**<sub>2</sub>_,...,_**b**_<sub>n</sub>_ form a basis of the lattice, and the matrix **B** with columns **b**<sub>1</sub>,**b**<sub>2</sub>_,...,_**b**_<sub>n</sub>_ is called a basis matrix.

**Definition 1** (Shortest Vector Problem (SVP))**.** _Given a lattice_ L_, the Shortest Vector Problem (SVP) asks for a shortest non-zero vector in the lattice, i.e.,_

\(\text{SVP}(\mathcal{L})=\text{argmin}\{\|\mathbf{v}\|_2|\mathbf{v}\in\mathcal{L},\mathbf{v}\neq\mathbf{0}\}\)

A standard notation for the length of the shortest vector in a lattice L is denoted by \(\lambda_1(\mathcal{L})\). In fact, a generalization of \(\lambda_1\) known as successive minima is defined as follows.

**Definition 2** (Successive minima)**.** _Given a lattice_ L _and_ \(i\in[n]\)_, the i<sup>th</sup> successive minima_ \(\lambda_i(\mathcal{L})\) _is defined as_

\(\lambda_i(\mathcal{L})=min\{r\in\mathbb{R}|\text{dim}(\text{span}(\mathcal{L}\cap\text{Ball}_{\ell_2}(0,r)))\ge i\}\)

Throughout the remainder of this section, unless stated otherwise, all norms are with respect to the \(\ell_2\)-norm.

**Definition 3** (Approximate Shortest Independent Vector Problem (SIVP))**.** _Given an n-dimensional lattice_ L _and an approximation function_ \(\gamma:\mathbb{N}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\)_, the_ \(\gamma\)_-approximate SIVP asks for n linearly independent vectors_ \(\mathbf{v}_1,\dots,\mathbf{v}_n\in\mathcal{L}\) _such that_ \(\|\mathbf{v}_i\|_2\le\gamma(n)\lambda_n(\mathcal{L})\) _for all_ \(i\in[n]\).

We consider the following variant of the above problem, which asks for a single vector.

**Definition 4** (Approximate _n<sup>th</sup>_-Successive Minima Problem (nSMP))**.** <sup>_10_</sup> _Given a lattice_ L _and an approximation function_ \(\gamma:\mathbb{N}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\)_, the_ \(\gamma\)_-approximate n<sup>th</sup> Successive Minima Problem (nSMP) asks for a non-zero vector_ **v** _in the lattice_ L _such that_ \(\|\mathbf{v}\|\le\gamma(n)\lambda_n(\mathcal{L})\).

Using Theorem B.3, one can show that any algorithm for \(\gamma(n)\)-approximate nSMP can be used to solve \(\sqrt{n}\gamma(n)\)-approximate SIVP.

<sup>10</sup>There is a well-studied lattice problem, called the _Successive Minima Problem_ (SMP) \[Mic08\], which asks for _n_ linearly independent lattice vectors **v**<sub>1</sub>_,...,_**v**_<sub>n</sub>_ such that \(\|\mathbf{v}_i\|=\lambda_i(\mathcal{L})\) for every \(i\in[n]\).

### 3.2 Hardness Hypothesis

For any parameter \(\kappa\ge 1\), the currently best algorithms for \(n^\kappa\)-approximate SVP run in \(2^{\mathcal{O}(n/\kappa)}\) time \[Sch87, SE94, GN08, ALNSD20\]. More precisely, when \(\kappa\ge 1\), \(n^\kappa\)-approximation to SVP can be computed in \(\mathcal{O}^\star(2^{0.802n/(\kappa+1)})\) time \[ALNSD20\]. Motivated by the apparent hardness, Vafa and Vaikuntanathan \[VV25\] implicitly stated the following hypothesis <sup>11</sup>:

**Hypothesis 2.** _For any_ \(\varepsilon>0\) _and parameter_ \(\ell\in[1,n]\)_, there is no_ \(2^{\mathcal{O}(n/\ell)^{1-\varepsilon}}\)_-time algorithm that given a lattice_ L _of dimension n returns n non-zero independent vectors_ \(\mathbf{v}_i\in\mathcal{L}\) _such that_ \(\|\mathbf{v}_i\|_2\le 2^{\mathcal{O}(\ell)}\cdot\lambda_n(\mathcal{L})\).

However, notice that since the work of Schnorr \[Sch87\], there is no 2<sup>_o(n_)</sup> time algorithm that solves _n<sup>c</sup>_-approximate SVP for any constant \(c\ge 0\). Motivated by this, we state an even stronger hypothesis than Hypothesis 2.

**Hypothesis 1.** _For any constant_ \(c\ge 1\)_, there exists_ \(\varepsilon>0\) _such that there is no_ \(\mathcal{O}(2^{\varepsilon n})\) _time algorithm that given an n-dimensional lattice_ L _with high probability returns a non-zero vector_ \(\mathbf{v}\in\mathcal{L}\) _such that_ \(\|\mathbf{v}\|_2\le\mathcal{O}(n^c)\cdot\lambda_n(\mathcal{L})\).

To the best of our knowledge, this hypothesis was not explicitly stated. However, if the hypothesis turns out to be false, it would mean a significant breakthrough on the approximate Shortest Vector Problem. In section Section B.1, we show that these problems are tightly connected.

## 8 Conclusion and Future Directions

We study the complexity of the Pigeonhole Equal Subset Sum and make progress on two central open questions: whether one can achieve subexponential-time algorithms and whether the O_<sup>⋆</sup>(M_<sup>1/3</sup>) barrier can be improved. Our contributions are

(i) Deterministic \(\mathrm{poly}(n)\cdot M^{\mathcal{O}(1/\mathrm{log}\delta)}\)-time algorithm when \(\delta=n/\mathrm{log}M\) is the density of the instance (Theorem 1.1).<tbc>

(ii) Conditional lower bound showing that no \(M^{o(1/\mathrm{log}\delta)}\)-time algorithm exists assuming currently based algorithms for lattice problems are tight (Theorem 1.2).<tbc>

(iii) Average-case, O_<sup>⋆</sup>_(2<sup>_n/_4</sup>)-time algorithms when \(M=\Theta(2^n)\) (Theorem 1.3 and Theorem 1.4)

Figure 2 gives a pictorial view of our results. We also show that no 2<sup>_o(n/_log_n_)</sup>-time algorithm exists for Pigeonhole Equal Subset Sum (conditionally answering open question of Jin [Jin24] up to log_n_ factor in the exponent).

Several intriguing directions remain open. Most notably, closing the remaining gap to fully resolve whether Pigeonhole Equal Subset Sum admits a 2<sup>_o(n_)</sup>-time algorithm remains a major challenge. Our lower bound relies on a technique of Vafa and Vaikuntanathan [VV25], who showed that no polynomial-time algorithm solves Number Balancing Problem with \(\kappa(n)=2^{-\Omega(\mathrm{log}^{3+\varepsilon}(n))}\). Although our lower bound is tight, it is tight only in the setting of exponential running times and does not improve the lower bound of Vafa and Vaikuntanathan [VV25]. In fact, our reduction, when plugged in with their hypothesis and parameters, would also exclude \(\kappa(n)=2^{-\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{log}^{3+\varepsilon}(n))}\)- approximation in polynomial time, but it would be worse because the lower bound of [VV25] prohibits even average-case algorithms. Can one improve these lower bounds in the setting of polynomial-time algorithms for Pigeonhole Equal Subset Sum?

Finally, we ask whether average-case algorithms for Pigeonhole Equal Subset Sum in the regime \(\delta=1\) can be extended to the worst-case setting. We conjecture that the structural insights of Jin, Williams, and Zhang [JWZ25] and our analysis in the average-case setting can be combined to yield an O_<sup>⋆</sup>_(2<sup>_n/_4</sup>)-time worst-case algorithm. Also, can we improve the average-case running time exponent of O_<sup>⋆</sup>_(2<sup>_n/_4</sup>) below 1/4?

## C Statistical Distance

**Lemma C.0.1.** _Let D_<sub>0</sub> _and D_<sub>1</sub> _be two distributions on the same sample space such that_ \(\Delta(D_0,D_1)\le\epsilon\)_. Consider the following two distributions on n-tuples._

• \(P:=D_0\times D_0\times\cdots\times D_0=D_0^n\).<tbc>

• _Q: sample independent uniform bits_ \(b_1,\dots,b_n\in\{0,1\}\)_, and then output an n-tuple whose i-th coordinate is sampled independently from D<sub>b<sub>i</sub></sub>._

_Then_ \(\Delta(P,Q)\le n\epsilon/2\).

_Proof._ We define hybrid distributions _H_<sub>0</sub>_,H_<sub>1</sub>_,...,H<sub>n</sub>_ by \(H_k:=D_1^k\times D_0^{n-k}\), for _k_=0,1_,...,n_. In particular, \(H_0=D_0^n=P\) and \(H_n=D_1^n\). However, the distribution _Q_ is not equal to _H<sub>n</sub>_. Instead, it is the product distribution<tbc>

\(Q=\left(\frac{D_0+D_1}{2}\right)^n,\)

<tbc>since each coordinate is sampled independently from _D_<sub>0</sub> or _D_<sub>1</sub> with equal probability. We now prove the desired bound by changing one coordinate at a time. Define<tbc>

\(G_k:=\left(\frac{D_0+D_1}{2}\right)^k\times D_0^{n-k},\)

<tbc>for _k_=0,1_,...,n_. Then _G_<sub>0</sub>=_P_ and \(G_n=\left(\frac{D_0+D_1}{2}\right)^n=Q\). By the triangle inequality,<tbc>

\(\Delta(P,Q)=\Delta(G_0,G_n)\le\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\Delta(G_k,G_{k+1}).\)

<tbc>Now _G<sub>k</sub>_ and _G_<sub>_k_+1</sub> differ only in the (_k_+1)-st coordinate, so<tbc>

\(\Delta(G_k,G_{k+1})=\Delta\left(D_0,\frac{D_0+D_1}{2}\right).\)

Using the definition of statistical distance, \(\Delta\big(D_0,\frac{D_0+D_1}{2}\big)=\frac{1}{2}\sum_x\big|D_0(x)-\frac{D_0(x)+D_1(x)}{2}\big|,\)
\(=\frac{1}{4}\sum_x|D_0(x)-D_1(x)|,\)
\(=\frac{1}{2}\Delta(D_0,D_1),\)
\(\le\frac{\epsilon}{2}.\) Therefore, \(\Delta(P,Q)\le\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\frac{\epsilon}{2}=\frac{n\epsilon}{2}.\) Notice that the hypothesis of Vafa and Vaikuntanathan \[VV25\] considered SIVP, whereas Hypothesis 2 concerns nSMP.
